questions.stem: A new hire in accounting is given access only to the accounting share and nothing else. Which security principle does this follow?
questions.explanation: Least privilege means a user or app gets only the minimum permissions needed to do the job - exactly the accounting-only access described.
questions.trap: Zero trust is the broader 'never trust by default' architecture; the specific act of granting minimum rights is least privilege.

questions.stem: A user logs in once in the morning and then reaches email, the file server, and the HR portal without re-entering a password. Which capability is in use?
questions.explanation: SSO is the master-key-card model: authenticate once, then access multiple applications without logging in again.
questions.trap: MFA strengthens a single login with extra factors; it does not by itself grant access across many apps.

questions.stem: A security architecture treats every request as untrusted and re-verifies it at every internal resource, not just at the network edge. What is this model called?
questions.explanation: Zero trust means nothing is trusted by default - like a security checkpoint at every internal door, not only the front entrance.
questions.trap: Least privilege is about how much access a verified identity gets; zero trust is about never assuming trust in the first place.

questions.stem: An admin needs elevated rights only for a 30-minute maintenance task, after which the rights automatically expire. Which PAM strategy provides this?
questions.explanation: Just-in-time access grants temporary, expiring admin rights, which prevents an attacker from gaining permanent control of a privileged account.
questions.trap: PAM is the overall vault for privileged accounts; just-in-time is the specific strategy of time-limited elevation.

questions.stem: A login requires a password plus a code from an authenticator app. Which two MFA factor categories are being combined?

choices.text: Somewhere you are and something you do
Something you are and somewhere you are
Something you have and something you are
Something you know and something you have

questions.explanation: A password is 'something you know'; the authenticator app on your phone generating a TOTP is 'something you have'.
questions.trap: A biometric would be 'something you are', but no biometric is used here - just a password and a phone app.

questions.stem: A system blocks employees from emailing files that contain credit-card numbers outside the company. Which control is this?
questions.explanation: DLP inspects data in motion and stops sensitive information like credit-card numbers from leaving the network.
questions.trap: MDM enforces policy on mobile devices; it is not the system that inspects outbound data for sensitive content.

questions.stem: An employee leaves the company and IT must remotely erase corporate data from their personal phone. Which tool provides this?
questions.explanation: MDM is the central console that can enforce policy and remotely wipe company data from a personal device when an employee leaves.
questions.trap: DLP stops data from leaving; it does not remotely wipe a device that already holds it.

questions.stem: A facility entrance only lets one person through at a time after a guard verifies them, preventing tailgating. What is this physical control called?
questions.explanation: An access control vestibule (mantrap) ensures only one verified person enters at a time, defeating tailgating.
questions.trap: Bollards stop vehicles; a magnetometer detects metal. Neither controls one-person-at-a-time entry.

questions.stem: Which biometric method is described as one of the MOST accurate because it reads the capillaries in the eye?
questions.explanation: A retina scanner reads the capillaries in the eye and is one of the most accurate biometrics.
questions.trap: Palm-print and voice recognition exist but are considered less secure. A smart card is a token, not a biometric.

questions.stem: A company wants web-app SSO using an open standard that confirms a user's identity with a trusted source before granting access. Which standard fits?
questions.explanation: SAML is the open standard often used to deliver SSO for web apps - acting like a digital valet that confirms identity with a trusted source.
questions.trap: RADIUS is a centralized AAA protocol for network access (Wi-Fi, VPN), not the web-app SSO standard described.
